name: Felix Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fine with me. I'm a straightforward bloke, so ask what you like.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm an improver carpenter with a regional housebuilder, which means I'm past labouring but not qualified yet. We're putting up forty detached houses on the old quarry site, and I do first fix: floor joists, stud partitions, helping lift the roof trusses with the crane. I like it when the roof's on and the house suddenly looks like a house. I don't like the target sheet; they pay a bonus per plot and I'm not quick enough to earn much of it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what's life like outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Hana, she's a teaching assistant at the primary school. We rent a small semi, and we've got about three weeks of money in the bank. My dad's a self-employed plasterer. My dad always says get your papers, son, nobody can take those off you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised; you can't build a house from a laptop. At the football on Sunday the lads would agree. Online I'd share a meme about it, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the same as now: get quicker, earn the bonus, get my papers. The housebuilder's steady as long as houses sell, and that depends on mortgage rates, not AI. If rates go up, they slow the site and juniors get cut first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the site manager again to put me on the formal apprenticeship, so I get the certificate. I'd do a few weekends with my dad when he's got a big job. I use AI now and then to check building regs and I'd keep doing that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit impatient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said rates matter more than AI. When did that last bite?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years ago the site went to three days a week for a couple of months because sales dried up. I did weekend plastering with my dad to make it up. I learned how quick three weeks of savings goes when the site went to three days a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why haven't they put you on the apprenticeship already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They say budget, they say next intake. I think they like having an improver who's cheap. I'd keep asking, politely, because that's how it's done.

I'd expect the lads at **Sunday football** to agree.
think: The housebuilder's steady work depends on **mortgage rates** and house sales, not AI.
If sales slow, **juniors get cut** first.
do: Ask again for the **formal apprenticeship** and its certificate.
Do **weekend plastering** with his dad on big jobs.
Keep using AI to check **building regs**.
feel: **Fine**, mostly, but **impatient** to get his papers.
S0.quote: I learned how quick three weeks of savings goes when the site went to three days a week.
fieldNote: His main risk is the **housing market**, not AI.
His dad's advice about **papers** shapes his whole plan.
He suspects the firm keeps him as a **cheap improver**.
He'd ask **politely**, in keeping with his traditional manner.

steps.text: Keep working first fix on the quarry site houses
Ask the site manager for a place on the formal apprenticeship
Plaster with his dad on weekends when big jobs come

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let the computers do the paperwork and leave the building to us. At work I'd say it should speed up the site office, not cut the trades. Online, not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's mostly fine for me, because first fix is all lifting and fixing. But the housebuilder will use AI to plan everything tighter and push the bonus targets up. I'm already struggling to hit them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the planning app once the other lads are on it, so I'm not the one holding things up. I'd push harder for the apprenticeship, and offer to do the college day on my own time if needed. And Hana and I would save fifty a week, starting now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like the targets are moving while I'm still learning to walk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the targets went up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the company really, they've got to compete. Maybe the government for not backing apprenticeships properly. A firm will always choose the cheap option if nobody rewards training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Hana say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say she's seen AI in the classroom already, marking spelling tests. She's not worried about her job, she says kids need a person. She'd tell me to stop moaning and get my papers.

fieldNote: He blames **weak apprenticeship support**, not his employer.

He follows others into tech, as a **steady adopter**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is mad and people need to slow down. At work we'd say robots can't lift trusses in the wind. Online I'd share stuff about protecting apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think 2031 is the end of first fix as a job for people like me. It's repetitive on a housing estate, same house type over and over. By then I'd be thirty-one with maybe half a certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 I'd ask my dad about going into plastering with him properly, because old houses are messy and he has regular customers. I'd use AI to price his jobs and do his invoices, which he hates. And Hana and I would hold off on buying a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried in my gut. Like a lift going down too fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't plastering hands-on work a robot could do too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On new builds, yes, probably. But in an old house with crumbling walls and a family living in it, I reckon a person lasts longer than a robot. That's my bet anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the lads on the site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to get their papers and get into repairs, not new builds. A robot on a housing estate is easy; a robot in somebody's front room is harder. Then I'd probably buy them a pint, because we'd all need one.

say: I'd say this is **mad** and people need to slow down.
I'd share posts online about **protecting apprenticeships** for young trades.
think: By **2031** first fix on estates ends as a job for people like him.
He'd be thirty-one with maybe **half a certificate**.
do: Join his **dad's plastering** business on old houses.
Use AI to **price and invoice** his dad's jobs.
Hold off on **buying a house** with his girlfriend.
feel: **Worried** in his gut, like a lift **going down** too fast.
S2.quote: In an old house with crumbling walls and a family living in it, I reckon a person lasts longer than a robot.
fieldNote: He judges **repetitive estate work** as an early robot target.
His fallback is the **family business** with regular customers.
He'd bring AI into his dad's **paperwork**, not the trade itself.
Family backup keeps him **anxious**, not alarmed.

steps.text: Join his dad's plastering business working on old houses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years means we can plan, so plan. At work I'd tell the young lads to get papers now. Online I'd keep sharing apprenticeship stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, eight years until robots means I can finish my papers and build up repair work. It's still scary, but it's a career path rather than a cliff. I'd be fine, I think, if I start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd push the housebuilder for the apprenticeship or leave for one elsewhere. I'd do weekends with Dad on repairs. And I'd start saving for a van, because you need your own van in repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but in a hopeful way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd leave for an apprenticeship. Would you really?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they kept saying next intake, yes. My dad would say go. Loyalty's good, but not to a firm that won't train you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the van mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Freedom, really. My own customers, my own name on the side. Dad says it's the day you stop being an employee.

I'd tell young lads to **get papers** now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, so no need to panic, just work hard. At work I'd say the same. Online, probably nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thirteen years until robots, I'd be forty with my papers and my own van. That's a life. I'd feel fairly secure, as long as houses keep needing fixing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, get the apprenticeship sorted and do weekends with Dad. I'd wait and see which AI tools the good repair firms use. And Hana and I would think about buying a small place in a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Still a bit on edge, because the bonus targets are still the bonus targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell yourself at forty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well done for getting your papers. And don't let your own kids skip theirs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still go wrong in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mortgage rates, a bad year for housing, the usual. Robots that far off are almost a relief compared to interest rates.

I'd say the same at work and **post nothing**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Housing estates are where robots start, and I'd have three years with half a certificate. What would help is a proper funded apprenticeship, so firms are rewarded for training, and a bit of help for small family businesses like my dad's.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my dad. He's fifty-five with bad knees, so if I go in with him it's partly to look after him too.

headlineQuote: My dad always says get your papers, son, nobody can take those off you.
portrait: Felix is **27**, an **improver carpenter** on a housing estate, waiting for an apprenticeship place.
He's **traditional**, values papers and family, and uses AI now and then for regs.
His steady worry is **mortgage rates** slowing the site, not technology.
AGI by **2028** pushes him toward his **dad's plastering** firm and old-house repairs.
With more time he plans **papers and a van** of his own.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with three years on estates and half a certificate.
whatWouldHelp: A **funded apprenticeship** that rewards training, plus help for **small family** firms.
